UI stands for user interface. It is what you can see and touch, the button, the colors, the layout, the icons, the screen.

UX, on the other hand, stands for user experience. It is how the old product feels to use. Can a user find what they're looking for? Does it make sense to the user? Did the users get frustrated using it? Did the user come back to use it?

The time was popularized by Don Norman back in the 80s when it was at Apple. And the way he and Jacob Nielsen describe it is that user experience cover every part of a person's interaction with a company, its services and its products.

The first big way to split UX research is generative versus evaluative. Generative UX research happens early, before anything is designed.
It asks questions like, "What is the real problem? What do people need? How do they get by right now without this thing that we are about to build?"
It generates ideas for what to build. For example, for my thesis, I'm doing generative research. Evaluative research, on the other hand, happens later, after there is a design.
It asks questions like, "Does this product actually work? Can users use it? Where do the users get stuck while using it?"
So you are evaluating something that already exists.
So generative UX research helps you decide what to build. And evaluative UX research tells you whether what you build works.
The second way to split UX research is qualitative versus quantitative. Quantitative UX research is about numbers.
How many people completed the task? What percentage dropped off at checkout? How long did it take? It tells you what is happening and how much of it.
Qualitative UX research is about understanding. Why did the users drop off? What were they thinking? What confused them?

It's usually smaller and more in depth. It tells you the why. Usually, you want both. You want the numbers to show where the problem is and you want the conversation to show why the problem is happening.
Now, the big way to split UX research is behavioral versus attitudinal. Attitudinal UX research is about what users say, what they think, what they feel, what they tell you that they do.
Surveys and interviews are mostly attitudinal. Behavioral UX research, on the other hand, is about what people actually do.
So you watch them use the thing. You look at the data on what they click.

The primary research is the research you do yourself, like running your own interview.
Secondary research uses what already exists, like published studies, industry reports and all of that.
Remote UX research happens over a video call through an online tool.
In-person research happens in the same room where you can notice things like body language and all of that.
And then we have moderated research, where a researcher is there, guiding the session, asking follow-up questions.
And unmoderated research, where people complete tasks on their own, usually through a tool that records them.
So how is UX research actually done? There are a lot of methods that I've actually mentioned in the earlier part.
There's user interview, where you sit down with people, you talk to them about their lives, their work, their frustration, maybe how they use their product and all of that.
There's usability testing. You give someone a task to do with your design, maybe with your app, you watch how they do the tasks, usually while they think out loud.
Then we have surveys. You can reach a lot of people quickly with surveys.

There are also diary studies, where people record their experiences over days or weeks, so you see patterns that maybe a single session would have missed.
